subject: Culture
title: The Death Positive Movement
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Death Positive Movement.

hook.text: Mortician Caitlin Doughty runs a YouTube channel about death that has 2 million subscribers. Death is trending.

buildup.text: The death positive movement advocates for open conversations about mortality, dying, and end-of-life planning.

discovery.text: Doughty founded the Order of the Good Death in 2011, arguing that death denial causes more suffering than death itself.

twist.text: Death cafes—casual gatherings to discuss mortality over tea—have held over 15,000 events in 80+ countries.

climax.text: The movement mirrors ancient traditions: cultures that talk about death consistently show lower death anxiety scores.

punchline.text: Hiding from death doesn't make it smaller. It makes it scarier.

quiz.question: Who founded the Order of the Good Death?

details.summary: The death positive movement, championed by mortician Caitlin Doughty and the Order of the Good Death, advocates for open conversation about death, the dying process, and the funeral industry. It fights death denial by encouraging people to plan their own deaths and question industry practices.
details.whyItMatters: Death positivity challenges a culture that spends billions hiding death from view. By making death a normal topic, the movement helps people make better end-of-life choices and grieve more healthily.
takeaways: Caitlin Doughty founded the Order of the Good Death in 2011
Death cafes — casual death discussion groups — now exist in 80+ countries
The movement advocates for transparency in the funeral industry

faq.question: What is a death cafe?
faq.answer: Death cafes are informal gatherings where strangers discuss death over tea and cake. Started by Jon Underwood in London in 2011, they now operate in over 80 countries. There is no agenda, therapy, or grief support — just open conversation about mortality.

faq.question: What does the death positive movement advocate?
faq.answer: Openness about death and dying, transparency in the funeral industry's pricing and practices, access to home funerals and green burial, advance directive planning, and cultural conversations about mortality.
